title: Separable algebraic base change preserves the maximal solvable normal subgroup
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field]. Group schemes, closed normal subgroups, smoothness, connectedness and finite type have the meanings of [def-sc-group-scheme, def-sc-group-scheme-subgroup, def-sbc-smooth-morphisms, def-weil-connected-scheme, def-weil-finite-type-morphism]. Geometrically connected means connected after extension to an algebraic closure [def-weil-algebraic-closure]. Let $G$ be a smooth geometrically connected affine $k$-group scheme of finite type, and let $R\subseteq G$ be a smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup containing every smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup of $G$. Here solvable means that the iterated derived subgroup eventually becomes trivial, and a derived subgroup is the smallest closed subgroup through which $(x,y)\mapsto xyx^{-1}y^{-1}$ factors. Let $K/k$ be a separable algebraic field extension [def-pc-field-extension]: every element of $K$ has a minimal polynomial over $k$ with no repeated roots in an algebraic closure. Write $G_K=G\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ and $R_K=R\times_{\operatorname{Spec}k}\operatorname{Spec}K$ [def-pc-fibre-product]. Then $R_K$ is smooth, connected, solvable and normal in $G_K$, and contains every smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup scheme of $G_K$. The extension need not be finite, and no reductivity hypothesis is imposed.

source.place: Proposition 19.1 and its proof, printed p.397, with 6.44 (p.135), Corollaries 6.19(a), 6.31 (pp.129,132). The separable algebraic extension is not restricted to finite extensions. No Stacks tag states this algebraic-group result.

proof.text: We first reconcile the two solvability conventions used by the cited statements. For a smooth connected affine group $H$, the product node makes $H$ geometrically connected. The derived-subgroup node applies successively to $H,D(H),D^2(H),\ldots$: all these groups are smooth and geometrically connected, their successive quotients are commutative, and $D^i(H)_M=D^i(H_M)$ for every field extension $M$. If $D^n(H)=1$, this is a solvable series in the convention of the product node. Conversely, for a solvable series $H=H_0\supseteq\cdots\supseteq H_n=1$, inductively $D^i(H)\subseteq H_i$: compose $D^i(H)\to H_i$ with the commutative quotient $H_i/H_{i+1}$, which is an affine group scheme of finite type by the normal-quotient node (applied to the normal closed subgroup $H_{i+1}$ of the affine finite-type group $H_i$); the derived-subgroup node kills its next derived subgroup. Thus $D^n(H)=1$. Finally, equality detection for closed subgroups shows $D^n(H_M)=1$ if and only if $D^n(H)=1$. Consequently solvability in the derived-series sense is preserved and reflected by every field extension for smooth connected affine groups.

Over any field $F$ and for any smooth geometrically connected affine finite-type group $J/F$, choose a smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup $U$ of greatest dimension. Such subgroups exist (the identity subgroup is one), and the product node bounds their integer dimensions by $\dim J$. For any other such subgroup $V$, the same node gives a smooth connected solvable normal closed product $UV$ containing $U,V$. If $U\ne UV$, strict dimension growth contradicts its choice. Hence $UV=U$ and $V\subseteq U$. This constructs a largest subgroup, denoted $\mathcal R_F(J)$, and proves its uniqueness. Step 1 makes this valid with precisely the solvability convention stated above. In particular $\mathcal R_k(G)=R$ by mutual containment.

source.place: 6.41--6.44, printed pp.134--135; the existence input recalled before 19.1, p.397.

proof.text: First let $L/k$ be Galois, allowing an infinite extension. Set $U=\mathcal R_L(G_L)$ using step 2. Each $\sigma\in\operatorname{Gal}(L/k)$ carries $U$ to another smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup of $G_L$: since $G$ is defined over $k$, $(G_L)\times_{\operatorname{Spec}L,\sigma}\operatorname{Spec}L=G_L$, and $\sigma(U)$ is the base change of $U$ along the field isomorphism $\sigma:L\to L$, which preserves the group law, all these properties and the derived series. Applying $\sigma^{-1}$ to the containment of any such subgroup proves that $\sigma(U)$ is again largest. Uniqueness gives $\sigma(U)=U$ as closed subgroup schemes, not merely on rational points; equivalently its defining ideal is stable under the canonical semilinear action. The Galois descent node therefore gives a unique closed subgroup $N\subseteq G$ with $N_L=U$. Its normality descends by that same node.

source.place: 19.1, printed p.397, and 1.54(a),(b), pp.21--22; 1.54(b) explicitly allows infinite Galois extensions.

proof.text: The descended $N$ is affine of finite type, being closed in the affine finite-type group $G$. The field-extension node gives a faithfully flat coordinate extension, both for $k\to L$ and for $k[N]\to L\otimes_k k[N]$. Surjectivity on spectra follows from the faithfully-flat spectrum node. The map $\operatorname{Spec}L\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ is quasi-compact since both are one-point spaces. Thus the smooth fpqc base-descent node applies to $N\to\operatorname{Spec}k$ and proves $N$ smooth from $N_L=U$ smooth. Also $|U|\to|N|$ is a continuous surjection, so $N$ is connected: a decomposition into two nonempty clopen pieces would pull back to such a decomposition of $U$. Step 1 now reflects solvability from $N_L=U$. We have proved every hypothesis needed to apply the defining maximality of $R$, and obtain $N\subseteq R$.

source.place: 19.1, printed p.397, descent of the subgroup properties; smooth descent: Stacks Tag 02VL (descent.tex, lemma-descending-property-smooth); faithfully flat spectra: Tag 00HP (algebra.tex, lemma-ff).

proof.text: The product node gives smoothness, connectedness and solvability of $R_L$, and the subgroup-descent node preserves normality under field extension. Thus the maximality of $U$ gives $R_L\subseteq U=N_L$. Inclusion detection yields $R\subseteq N$. Together with step 4 this gives $N=R$ and $U=R_L$. This proves the full assertion for every Galois extension, including infinite ones; no finite-generation descent of $U$ to a finite subextension is being assumed.

source.place: 19.1, printed p.397, two containments; 1.54(b), printed p.22, for the infinite extension.

proof.text: For the given separable algebraic $K/k$, choose a separable closure $\Omega/k$ by the separable-closure node, and use the embedding node to embed $K$ into $\Omega$ over $k$. Identify $K$ with its image. The separable-closure node says $\Omega/k$ is Galois. Step 5 therefore gives $R_\Omega=\mathcal R_\Omega(G_\Omega)$. Let $V\subseteq G_K$ be any smooth connected solvable normal closed subgroup. The product node and normality base-change detection give the same properties for $V_\Omega\subseteq G_\Omega$. Hence $V_\Omega\subseteq R_\Omega=(R_K)_\Omega$. Apply closed-subgroup inclusion detection to the extension $\Omega/K$ to conclude $V\subseteq R_K$. There is no requirement that $K/k$ be finite or normal.

source.place: 19.1, printed p.397, passage to a Galois overfield; separable closures and their embeddings: Stacks Tags 09GT, 09HC, 09GU, 09I2, fields.tex, as specified by the cited field nodes.

proof.text: Finally $R_K$ itself is smooth, connected and solvable by the product node (using the equivalence established in step 1), and normal by the normality base-change clause of the subgroup-descent node. It is a closed subgroup by base change of its defining ideal. Step 6 proves that it contains every subgroup required here, which completes all its clauses.
